To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the star formation rates (SFRs) of starburst galaxies are underestimated if only CO(1-0) is observed, and the SFRs are overestimated if only HCN is observed; (ii) the CO(2-1) and HCN(1-0)/CO(1-0), HCO+(1-0)/HCN(1-0, and HCN(3-2)/CO(3-2) line ratios are good

(a) the star formation rate (SFR) of the galaxy can be estimated from the HCN line intensity, (b) the HCN-to-HCO line ratio is correlated with the metallicity of the galaxy, (c) the CO-to-HCN ratio is correlated with metallicity and SFR, and (d) the dust temperature is higher in the central regions than in the outer regions of the galaxies

1) the star formation efficiency of molecular clouds (SFE) is a strong function of the metallicity of the galaxy; 2) the SFE is also strongly affected by the environment of the cloud; 3) the star formation rate of the galaxy is a strong function the metallicity; 4) the SFE and the star formation rate are both strong functions of the environment.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
we have been successful to trace star formation in galaxies by using molecular line and continuum data.
the current data are consistent with a picture in which the star formation rate in the disk is proportional to the gas surface density.
the molecular line observations have been very successful in tracing the star formation in the nearby galaxies, but the continuum observations have not been so successful.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed the tools for studying star formation in galaxies at various stages, from starburst to quiescent, and in various environments, such as in the center and outskirts of galaxies.
we are now able to trace star formation in galaxies from molecular gas, dust, star-forming regions, young stars and old stars.

we have been studying the molecular line and continuum emissions in nearby star forming galaxies, and have been trying to understand the star formation processes in these galaxies by comparing the observed data with theoretical models.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the CO(1-0) luminosity of a galaxy can be used as a good tracer of star formation.
extragalactic observations can be used to study the star formation process.
molecular gas tracers are excellent tools to trace star formation and to understand how it relates to the physical conditions of the ISM.
